problem: "TLS works this way" is no longer accurate. Modern TLS (1.3) does not have the sender encrypt a random session key with the receiver's public key; the two sides agree the session key with an (elliptic-curve) Diffie–Hellman exchange. Only older TLS versions used RSA key transport.
fix: "Older TLS versions work exactly this way (RSA key transport). TLS 1.3 instead agrees the session key with a Diffie–Hellman exchange, but the hybrid pattern is unchanged: one slow public-key step fixes the key, a fast symmetric cipher carries the data."

where: Section 1, trapdoor permutation sentence, and Exam trap 5
problem: "A bijection, meaning every y has exactly one x" describes only the one-to-one half. A bijection from X to Y must also be onto: every y in Y must be the image of some x. As written, a student can call any injective function a permutation.
fix: "When f is a bijection from X to Y — one-to-one (no two inputs share an output) and onto (every y in Y is f(x) for some x) — so every y has exactly one preimage, some syllabi call f a trapdoor permutation." Apply the same wording in Exam trap 5.

where: Figure and Worked example 1 (n = 55, e = 3, d = 27)
problem: The figure and the example say reversing x³ mod 55 without the trapdoor is infeasible, but the modulus is 55, so a student can list all 55 outputs and invert by hand in a minute. With tiny numbers the security claim is false; only the arithmetic is being illustrated.
fix: Add one sentence before the example: "The numbers here are tiny so the arithmetic can be checked by hand; with n = 55 the inverse is findable by trial, and the infeasibility appears only at real sizes, for example a 2048-bit modulus."
